newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition to protest through holiday.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition to protest through holiday.

text.p: Demonstrators planned to take to the streets of Belgrade again on Friday as an eruption of protest against alleged election fraud turned increasingly into a bid to overthrow President Slobodan Milosevic.

Activists for the opposition coalition Zajedno (Together) admitted they faced an uphill battle to maintain the momentum of the past week, in which between 50,000 and 100,000 people jammed the city streets daily, through the Republic Day long weekend.

Heavy snow was forecast for Friday. But activists insisted that if their supporters could put up with the driving rain that washed the rallies earlier in the week, they would come in strength even on a public holiday when Belgraders traditionally leave for winter resorts.
"We have already set in motion the process of changes and reforms -- the victory in Belgrade is simply the beginning," a Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic told Thursday's crowd.
"There are enough of us, and we have the necessary strength and energy. Our programme is to make free people out of you."

The protesters have filled the streets daily ever since electoral commissions controlled by the ruling Socialist Party overturned clear opposition victories in local council elections across the country almost two weeks ago.
Zajedno has seized on its unexpected wave of support, turning it into a mass movement demanding president Slobodan Milosevic's resignation.
The coalition strategists said they planned to keep the demonstrations rolling through at least to Tuesday, when the Serbian parliament holds its next session.

Then they say Zajedno will surround the parliament with what they hope will be their biggest mass rally yet, to add weight to demands that the parliament recognises their "stolen" local election wins and hands over Milosevic's political scalp.
One senior strategist, former foreign minister Ilija Djukic, said Zajedno had tapped a well of boiling frustration.
"It is obvious that the citizens are ripe for a change," he told Reuters.

"They are motivated not by support for Zajedno, but because of real problems -- the terrible economic situation, Yugoslavia's international isolation and the rejection of already compromised authorities."
Milosevic had looked well on the way to burying his political opponents and rehabilitating himself with Western powers until he blatantly cancelled the opposition victories.
Diplomats say Milosevic has now shattered any surviving credentials he may have had as a democrat by moving to gag media coverage of the protests.
Belgrade's independent radio station B-92 accused the authorities of jamming its news broadcasts and live reports from the rallies.
Journalists from both independent and state-backed Serbian newspapers have complained of attempts to trivialise their reporting of the protests.

"We are not advocates of partial journalism but are for the respect of facts and events which are unfolding before the eyes of our readers," wrote journalists from the state-sponsored Politika newspaper in a letter to its editorial board.
Rather than sweeping the previously fractured opposition aside, Milosevic's annulment of the election results breathed life into the coalition partners and gave them a common goal.
"It was a miscalculation," Djindjic told Reuters.

"He had the chance to minimise the importance of the local elections...to prevent us from exerting real authority at the municipal level and to let the defeat pass quietly. Instead, he turned the local elections into presidential elections."
